title: Adaptive slice tiler and power-steered scheduling for attention on H100/L40S
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Background: We observe variable tail latency on multi-tenant H100/L40S hosts when serving medium-length chat workloads (avg seq length 512). Root cause analysis points to two interacting factors: (1) slice-level heterogeneity from dynamic MIG partitioning (hot slices hitting higher GPU clocks versus colder slices), and (2) suboptimal attention tiling + kernel selection that doesn't adapt to slice power states and KV cache occupancy during prefill -> decode transitions.

Goal: Reduce 95th percentile token latency by 20% for seq_len ~512 workloads across mixed MIG partitions without increasing average cost/token by more than 7%. Enable a scheduler that adapts kernel selection and attention tile sizes to slice clock state and observed token-density patterns (prefill vs. decode).

Proposed design:
- Slice telemetry enrichment: extend existing hw telemetry to export per-MIG-slice clock governor state, temperature, and active SM fraction to the runtime router. Add a lightweight burst window metric that flags slices in boosted vs. throttled states.
- Adaptive tile selector: implement a runtime component that chooses attention tiling (QKV tiling/blocking) and kernel variant (small-block vs. large-block matmul kernels) based on three signals: slice clock state, current KV cache occupancy, and batch token density. The selector uses a tiny decision table derived from offline microbench results and falls back to default kernel if signals conflict.
- Prefill->Decode handoff policy: introduce an explicit handoff stage where prefill windows are chunked to align with chosen tile sizes; decode requests use a 'warm-start hint' referencing the tile layout used during prefill to avoid kernel reconfiguration thrash. This handshake is recorded in request metadata (runtime-only; not persisted).
- Clock-aware packing: when placing concurrent workloads on slices, the scheduler prefers packings that minimize mixing boosted and throttled slices for the same KV-cache-heavy model. If unavoidable, prefer scheduling decode-heavy, low-throughput jobs on throttled slices and prefill-heavy on boosted slices.

Trade-offs considered:
- Complexity vs. latency wins: the adaptive selector adds control-path logic and extra telemetry which increases scheduler complexity and marginal CPU overhead. We cap that overhead (<2% CPU on control plane) and keep decision path O(1).
- Conservative rollout vs. aggressive perf: start with read-only telemetry and decision-table experiments (no enforced packing changes) to measure wins, then enable enforcement via a rollout feature flag.

Success metrics:
- 95th percentile token latency reduction >= 20% for target workloads on H100/L40S in lab.
- Average cost/token change <= +7% across synthetic and customer-like workloads.
- No regression in error rate or tail OOM events.

Operational plan / rollout:
1) Lab microbenching (2 weeks): capture kernel-level latencies across tile sizes on H100/L40S/A10 with MIG partitions (1g.5gb, 2g, 3g). Produce decision tables and validate warm-start hints reduce kernel reconfig events.
2) Staged Canary (2 weeks): enable telemetry + adaptive selector for internal-canary orgs, read-only mode first (log chosen kernel), compare logs to decision-table predictions.
3) Controlled rollout (2 cycles): enable packing policy and handoff hints for 10% traffic, monitor latency and cost dashboards (dashboard link below).
4) Full rollout if metrics stable.

Implementation notes:
- PRs: runtime decision-table and selector in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/12345, telemetry exporter in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/telemetry/pull/678.
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwoodinternal.com/display/INF/Adaptive+Slice+Tiler+Design

Open questions:
- How to encode warm-start hints in the public API without leaking runtime internals? Current plan is to keep hints internal to the serving router and not expose externally.
- For on-prem customers with static MIG configs, can we precompute optimal tables offline and skip telemetry? Likely yes; need a small installer step for private deploys.
